prompt_title: Should Schools Teach Mindfulness?
text:
Schools should teach mindfulness, but they should do it carefully and realistically. Students today face a lot of pressure: grades, friendships, family problems, social media, and worries about the future. Many young people are constantly distracted or stressed, and they are not always taught simple ways to calm their minds or understand their emotions. Mindfulness can be one useful tool for that.

I have tried mindfulness in small ways, such as taking a few minutes to focus on breathing or noticing what I am feeling without immediately reacting. It can feel awkward at first, especially if you are used to being busy all the time. But after a while, it can also feel grounding. It does not magically solve problems, but it can create a little space between a feeling and a response. For students, that space could help them handle anxiety before a test, calm down after an argument, or pay better attention in class.

However, schools should not treat mindfulness as a cure-all. It should not replace counselors, smaller class sizes, good teaching, or real support for students who are struggling. It should also not be forced in a way that makes students uncomfortable. Some students may not want to close their eyes, sit still, or participate because of personal, cultural, religious, or trauma-related reasons. Schools should offer choices, explain that mindfulness is a practical attention and stress-management skill, and avoid presenting it as a spiritual requirement.

A good approach would be brief and simple: a few minutes of breathing, quiet reflection, stretching, or noticing one’s thoughts before class begins or before a stressful activity. Teachers would need proper training so it does not become just another trend.

Overall, mindfulness belongs in schools if it is optional, inclusive, and taught as one tool among many. Students learn math, reading, and science because those skills help them live better lives. Learning how to pause, focus, and manage emotions can be just as important.

prompt_title: How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time
text:
We should be worried about screen time during the pandemic, but not in the same way we were before. The old debate often treated screens as if they were automatically harmful and “real life” as something that happened only away from devices. During the pandemic, that distinction became much less useful. Screens became classrooms, offices, birthday parties, therapy rooms, religious services and dinner tables. For many people, they were not a distraction from life but a lifeline to it.

Because of that, I do not think we should feel guilty simply because our screen hours increased. A child attending online school, a parent working remotely and a grandparent video-calling family are not all doing the same thing as someone scrolling endlessly through arguments and bad news. The purpose of screen use matters. So does the way it makes us feel afterward. If a screen helps us learn, earn a living, stay informed or feel less alone, then it is serving an important purpose.

Still, we should not “get over” the issue completely. Too much screen time can affect sleep, attention, mood and physical health, especially when it replaces movement, rest or face-to-face relationships within the home. The pandemic also made it easier to fall into unhealthy habits: constant news checking, late-night scrolling, comparing our lives to others, or using entertainment to avoid every uncomfortable feeling. Those patterns deserve concern.

The better question is not how many hours we spend on screens, but what kind of life our screen use supports. We should make room for breaks, outdoor time, exercise, reading, boredom and real conversation. We should also protect sleep by keeping devices away at night when possible. But we should stop pretending that all screen time is the same.

During the pandemic, screens helped us survive isolation. The goal now should not be panic or blind acceptance, but balance. We can be grateful for digital technology while still setting boundaries around it.

prompt_title: How Do You Think Technology Affects Dating?
text:
Technology has changed dating in both helpful and harmful ways. I do not have personal experience with dating or dating apps, but I can see how much they shape the way people meet, talk and build relationships today. In my opinion, technology makes dating easier to start but sometimes harder to sustain.

Dating apps can be useful because they introduce people who might never meet in daily life. Someone who is shy, busy or new to an area can find potential partners quickly. Apps also allow people to be clear about what they want, whether that is a serious relationship, casual dating or friendship. In this way, technology can create more opportunities and make dating feel less limited by location or social circles.

At the same time, dating apps can make people seem disposable. When there are hundreds of profiles to swipe through, it is easy to judge someone too quickly or keep looking for a “better” option. This can make romantic interactions feel less sincere. People may put more effort into presenting a perfect image than into being honest. Rejection can also feel constant and impersonal.

Texting and social media have similar effects. Texting helps couples stay connected throughout the day, especially when they are busy or far apart. However, it can also create misunderstandings because tone is hard to read. A late reply or a short message can cause anxiety, even when nothing is wrong. Social media can add pressure too. Couples may compare their relationship to idealized pictures online, or they may argue over likes, comments and who follows whom.

Technology like Netflix can improve relationships when it gives couples easy ways to relax together. But if people only sit in front of screens and stop having real conversations, it can weaken closeness.

Overall, I think technology is neither completely good nor bad for dating. It depends on how people use it. It can help people meet and stay connected, but it cannot replace honesty, patience and face-to-face communication. Those are still the most important parts of any strong relationship.

prompt_title: What Stereotypical Characters Make You Cringe?
text:
The stereotypical characters that make me cringe most are the ones that reduce a whole group of people to a single joke, accent, trauma, or personality trait. I especially dislike the “sassy best friend” who exists only to support the main character, the “model minority” who is portrayed as brilliant but emotionless, and the “angry woman” whose legitimate frustration is treated as irrational. These characters feel lazy because they do not seem like real people. They feel like shortcuts a writer used instead of doing the work of creating someone complex.

I also cringe at portrayals of poor people as either noble saints or irresponsible fools. In many stories, poverty is used as decoration, either to make a character seem inspirational or to blame them for their own situation. Real life is much more complicated than that. The same is true for characters with disabilities who are written only to teach others a lesson, or LGBTQ characters who are included just to suffer, die, or provide comic relief. When a character’s identity is treated as a plot device rather than a human experience, it becomes uncomfortable to watch.

I do not think every offensive portrayal has to make me immediately stop reading or watching. Sometimes older works reflect the prejudices of their time, and it can be useful to think critically about them. Sometimes a story may include a stereotype on purpose in order to challenge it. But if a movie, show, or book seems to enjoy the stereotype, or if it keeps punching down without any awareness, I would probably stop. Entertainment does not have to be perfect, but it should show some respect for the people it represents.

For me, the issue is not that characters must be flawless or politically correct. People can be messy, funny, cruel, strange, or wrong. The problem is when they are not allowed to be fully human. A good character can surprise us. A stereotype only repeats what we have already heard.

prompt_title: Is It Wrong to Focus on Animal Welfare When Humans Are Suffering?
text:
It is not surprising that many people feel especially strong empathy for animals. Animals seem innocent in a way that adults often do not. A dog or cat cannot explain itself, defend itself in words, or be blamed for its situation. When we hear that an animal has been abused, we may imagine a helpless creature that trusted humans and was betrayed. With people, our reactions are often more complicated. We may wonder about the circumstances, the person’s choices, or our own distance from the victim. Those thoughts can reduce immediate sympathy, even when they should not.

People also form deep emotional bonds with animals. A pet is not an abstract symbol; it is part of daily life. It greets us, depends on us, and offers affection without judgment. By contrast, human suffering in the news can feel overwhelming and remote. Wars, poverty, homelessness, and illness are so large that people may become numb. Caring for animals can seem more manageable: donate to a shelter, adopt a pet, report cruelty. The problem feels smaller and closer.

I do not think it is wrong to focus on animal welfare while humans are suffering. Compassion is not a limited resource in the simple sense that loving animals means hating people. A society that teaches kindness toward vulnerable creatures may also become more sensitive to human cruelty and neglect. Animal welfare matters because animals can feel pain, fear, hunger, and loneliness. Their suffering is real, even if it is different from human suffering.

However, it would be wrong to use concern for animals as an excuse to ignore people. If someone cares deeply about abused dogs but feels nothing for refugees, prisoners, or the poor, that imbalance deserves questioning. Human beings also suffer terribly, and their lives have moral weight. The best response is not to rank suffering in a cruel competition. We should widen our circle of concern. Caring about animals should make us more compassionate, not less, toward humans.

prompt_title: Are We Being Bad Citizens If We Don't Keep Up With the News?
text:
I do not think people are automatically bad citizens if they do not keep up with the news every day. Modern news can be overwhelming, repetitive and emotionally exhausting. A person who is working long hours, caring for family or struggling with their own health may not have the time or energy to follow every political debate, crisis or scandal. It would be unfair to call that person a bad citizen simply because they are not constantly informed.

However, I do think citizens have some responsibility to know what is going on around them, especially in their own community and country. Democracy depends on people making choices, and those choices are better when they are based on facts rather than rumors or vague feelings. If we vote without knowing anything about the candidates, ignore laws that affect our neighbors or refuse to learn about major problems, then we make it easier for powerful people to act without accountability. In that sense, total ignorance can become a civic failure.

Engaging with current events does not always produce immediate results. Reading an article about climate change or a war will not, by itself, solve anything. But awareness can still matter. It can shape how we vote, what we buy, what causes we support and how we talk to others. It can also help us recognize injustice when it happens. Social change often begins with people paying attention before they take action.

At the same time, keeping up with the news should not mean living in a constant state of outrage. Being informed is different from being addicted to headlines. A good citizen can set limits, choose reliable sources and focus on issues that truly matter. We do not need to know every detail of every event, but we should make a sincere effort to understand the world we share with other people. Citizenship is not just a legal status; it is a relationship with society. Paying attention is one way of honoring that relationship.

prompt_title: Is Listening to a Book Just as Good as Reading It?
text:
Listening to a book can be just as good as reading it, depending on the purpose and the person. I do listen to audiobooks, and I think they are one of the best ways to make books fit into a busy life. They allow people to enjoy stories and ideas while driving, walking, cooking, cleaning, or exercising. For many readers, audiobooks turn wasted time into meaningful time.

One major benefit of listening is that a good narrator can bring a book to life. Tone, pacing, accents, and emotion can make dialogue clearer and scenes more vivid. This is especially true for memoirs read by the author or novels with strong voices. Listening can also make difficult books feel more approachable, because the rhythm of speech helps carry the listener through complicated passages.

However, reading has advantages that listening cannot fully replace. When I read a printed book or an e-book, I control the pace more easily. I can stop, reread a sentence, underline a passage, or pause to think. This is especially useful for dense nonfiction, poetry, philosophy, or any book where the exact wording matters. Reading also demands a certain kind of focus. With audiobooks, it is easy for my attention to drift if I am doing something else at the same time. I may realize I missed an important paragraph and have to rewind.

I do not think listening is “cheating.” If someone understands, enjoys, and reflects on a book, then they have experienced it in a real way. Stories began as oral traditions long before printed books became common, so listening is not a lesser form. It is simply a different form.

Personally, I prefer reading for serious or complex books and listening for novels, memoirs, and lighter nonfiction. If I had to choose only one, I would choose reading because I like the quiet concentration it requires. But I am glad I do not have to choose. The best method is the one that keeps people connected to books.

prompt_title: Should College Athletes Be Paid?
text:
College athletes should be allowed to be paid, especially when their work helps generate millions of dollars for universities, television networks, coaches, and athletic departments. A scholarship is valuable, and for many students it can be life-changing. But it does not fully answer the fairness problem. Some athletes spend as much time on their sport as they would on a full-time job, while also facing injury risks and limits on their ability to earn money in other ways. If everyone around them can profit from their talent, it seems unfair to say that the athletes themselves should be the only ones who cannot.

Cody J. McDavis makes a reasonable point that direct salaries could create problems. If colleges simply started bidding for athletes, the richest programs would have an even bigger advantage. Smaller schools might feel pressure to spend money they do not have, and non-revenue sports could be harmed if athletic departments shifted resources toward football and basketball. There would also be difficult questions about fairness: Should star quarterbacks be paid more than swimmers or volleyball players? Should men’s and women’s teams be paid the same? These are serious concerns.

Still, I do not think these difficulties prove that athletes should receive no compensation. They show that the system needs rules. For example, athletes should be able to earn money from their name, image, and likeness, through endorsements, sponsorships, camps, or social media. This allows players to benefit from their own value without requiring every college to pay large salaries. Schools could also provide stronger health insurance, injury protection, travel support, and modest stipends for living expenses.

College sports should not become only a marketplace where the richest schools buy all the talent. But the old idea of amateurism is hard to defend when college sports are already a major business. A fair system would protect education and competitive balance while recognizing that athletes deserve more than applause, exposure, and a scholarship.

prompt_title: Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
text:
Pursuing risky sports like extreme mountain climbing is not automatically selfish, but it can become selfish depending on how a person prepares, what responsibilities they have, and how their choices affect others. Risk is part of life, and it is certainly part of sport. People can be injured playing football, skiing, cycling, or even running. If we judged every activity only by the possibility of harm, we would have to give up many experiences that make life meaningful.

Extreme climbing, however, is different from ordinary risk because the margin for error can be extremely small. A sudden storm, an avalanche, a mistake with equipment, or a moment of exhaustion can mean death not only for the climber but also for guides, teammates, and rescuers. That is where the ethical question becomes serious. A person may have the right to risk his or her own life, but no one has the right to casually endanger others or leave behind responsibilities without thought.

The line between reasonable and unreasonable risk should be drawn by asking several questions. Has the athlete trained properly? Is the equipment reliable? Is the person honest about the danger, or driven by ego and publicity? Are there children, partners, or dependents who would suffer greatly if the athlete died? Is the climb being attempted in conditions that experienced people consider reckless? Risk taken with discipline and respect is very different from risk taken for attention.

I do not think a sport stops being a sport simply because it is dangerous. Extreme mountain climbing requires skill, endurance, judgment, and courage. But calling something a sport should not excuse every decision made in its name. Some attempts are admirable; others are irresponsible.

In the end, risky sports are not selfish when pursued thoughtfully, with preparation and concern for others. They become selfish when the thrill matters more than the consequences. Freedom to take risks should come with humility, responsibility, and a clear understanding that courage is not the same as carelessness.

prompt_title: What Are the Most Important Things Students Should Learn in School?
text:
Schools should teach more than facts for tests. In my opinion, the most important things students should learn are how to think clearly, communicate well, work with others, and keep learning even when something is difficult. Subjects like math, science, history, and literature matter because they give students knowledge about the world. But the deeper purpose of these subjects is to help students ask good questions, understand evidence, solve problems, and see life from different points of view.

Students should also learn practical skills. They should know how to manage money, use technology responsibly, take care of their health, and understand their rights and responsibilities as citizens. Just as importantly, school should help students build character. Patience, honesty, respect, and perseverance are not always listed as lessons, but they are essential for a good life. A student who knows how to handle failure and keep trying will be better prepared than one who only knows how to memorize information.

The most important thing I have learned in school is that effort can change ability. I used to think that being “good” at something meant it should come easily. School taught me that improvement often comes slowly, through practice, mistakes, and feedback. This lesson affected my life because it made me less afraid of challenges. Instead of giving up when I do not understand something right away, I try different methods, ask for help, and keep working.

I believe this knowledge will help my success in the future because life will always bring new problems. Jobs change, technology changes, and people face unexpected difficulties. If I know how to learn, adapt, and continue after setbacks, I can handle those changes more confidently. In the end, the most important education is not just remembering information, but becoming a person who can think, grow, and contribute to others.

prompt_title: Should Schools Teach Mindfulness?
persona: a retired secondary school teacher who values tradition and discipline
text:
I have never been one for fashionable educational cures. In my years teaching secondary school, I saw many ideas arrive with great enthusiasm and disappear just as quickly, leaving teachers to tidy up the consequences. Schools, in my view, exist to teach knowledge, good habits, self-control and respect. They are not clinics, and teachers should not be expected to solve every emotional difficulty a child may face.

That said, I would not dismiss mindfulness entirely. Quiet reflection, steady breathing and learning to pause before reacting are not foolish ideas. In fact, they are close to what older generations might simply have called composure. A pupil who can sit still, listen carefully and control his temper is better prepared to learn. I remember many lessons in which five minutes of silence would have done more good than another lecture from me about behaviour.

However, I would be cautious about making mindfulness a major part of the school day. Time is limited. Many pupils already leave school unable to write clearly, calculate confidently or concentrate on a demanding text. If mindfulness means replacing English, mathematics, history or science, then I am firmly against it. Nor should it be presented in a vague or spiritual manner that makes families uncomfortable. Schools serve pupils from many backgrounds, and they must be careful not to impose beliefs under a new name.

If used at all, mindfulness should be practical, brief and disciplined. A form tutor might begin the day with a minute of silence, or a teacher might ask a restless class to breathe, settle and prepare for work. That is quite different from turning lessons into therapy sessions. The aim should be to support learning, not distract from it.

So yes, schools may teach a modest form of mindfulness, provided it is sensible, secular and subordinate to the main business of education. Children need calm minds, but they also need firm expectations, orderly classrooms and a serious curriculum. Mindfulness should serve those aims, not replace them.

prompt_title: How Worried Should We Be About Screen Time
persona: a retired secondary school teacher who values tradition and discipline
text:
I do not think we should panic about screen time during the pandemic, but neither do I think we should surrender our judgment to it. Screens have been useful, even necessary. Children have attended lessons, grandparents have seen their grandchildren, and workers have kept their jobs because of them. It would be foolish to deny that. In a crisis, we use the tools available.

Still, necessity is not the same as virtue. As a retired secondary school teacher, I have seen too many young people lose the habits that help them grow: attention, patience, neatness, self-control and the ability to sit quietly with a difficult task. Screens often work against these habits. They encourage speed, distraction and constant entertainment. A pupil who can flick from a lesson to a game to a message in a matter of seconds is not being trained in discipline. He is being trained in restlessness.

During the pandemic, some extra screen use was unavoidable, and parents should not be made to feel guilty for relying on it. A child doing algebra online or speaking to a lonely aunt is not wasting time. But we should still make distinctions. There is a difference between using a device as a tool and letting it become the master of the household. Online lessons, reading, music practice with a video teacher, or a family call are very different from endless scrolling and gaming late into the night.

The answer, as with most things in education and family life, is order. Set hours. Keep meals screen-free. Insist that phones are put away at bedtime. Encourage books, walks, chores, conversation and, when possible, handwritten work. Children need boundaries even more in unsettled times.

So yes, we should be concerned, but not hysterical. Screens have helped us through a hard season, and we should be grateful. But when ordinary life returns, we must not forget that young people are formed not only by what they know, but by the habits they keep.

prompt_title: How Do You Think Technology Affects Dating?
persona: a retired secondary school teacher who values tradition and discipline
text:
I have been married for many years, so my personal experience of dating belongs to a different age. When I was young, a fellow had to make an effort. He telephoned the house, spoke politely to a parent, arrived on time, and made clear his intentions by his conduct. A young woman, too, learned much from whether he kept his word, dressed properly, and treated others with respect. There was a certain order to it, and that order served a purpose.

I have never used dating apps, nor do I expect I ever shall. From what I hear from former pupils and younger relatives, these apps can be convenient, but convenience is not the same as wisdom. They seem to encourage people to judge one another quickly, often by photographs and clever little phrases. That may help two people meet, but it can also make them careless. When there is always another possible match waiting on a screen, it becomes easier to give up at the first disappointment.

Texting has similar problems. It is useful for arranging a time or saying one is running late, but serious matters should be discussed face to face. Too many young people try to conduct entire relationships through short messages, emojis, and late-night chats. Tone is misunderstood, feelings are hidden, and courage is avoided. In my classroom, I used to tell students that discipline is doing the right thing even when it is uncomfortable. That applies to love as much as to homework.

Social media also creates unnecessary comparison. Couples perform happiness for an audience, and private matters become public entertainment. Even a quiet evening together can be spoiled if both people are half-watching Netflix and half-scrolling through their phones.

Still, I do not believe technology is all bad. It can help lonely people find one another, especially in a busy world. But it must be kept in its proper place. Technology should assist courtship, not replace character, patience, manners, and honest conversation. Without those old-fashioned virtues, romance becomes shallow, no matter how modern the tools may be.

prompt_title: What Stereotypical Characters Make You Cringe?
persona: a retired secondary school teacher who values tradition and discipline
text:
I have spent most of my life around young people, and one thing teaching taught me is that careless labels stick. For that reason, the stereotypical characters that make me cringe most are the ones written as if a whole group of people can be summed up in one lazy joke. I dislike the “hopeless old fool” who exists only to be mocked for not understanding modern life. Age does not make a person useless, any more than youth makes a person wise. I also dislike the “strict teacher” or “stern parent” who is always shown as cruel, joyless and secretly ridiculous. Discipline, properly given, is not bullying. Standards are not hatred. Many children need firm boundaries before they can discover their talents.

I also find it tiresome when working-class people are portrayed as ignorant brutes, or when immigrants are reduced to funny accents and confusion. In my classroom I taught pupils from many backgrounds, and the serious ones all wanted much the same thing: a chance to learn, to be respected, and to make their families proud. When a film turns them into cartoons, it is not only unkind but untrue.

That said, I do not believe every unpleasant character is offensive. Literature and drama must be allowed to show foolishness, vice and prejudice. A story with no sharp edges is not much of a story. The question is whether the writer has observed human beings honestly, or merely reached for a cheap shortcut.

Would I refuse to watch or read something because of this? Yes, if the portrayal were consistently mean-spirited and added nothing except contempt. I have no patience, in retirement or otherwise, for entertainment that encourages people to sneer at their neighbours. But I would not abandon a serious work simply because it contains prejudice. Sometimes we must look at ugly things directly in order to understand them. Good art should enlarge our sympathies, not train us to laugh at people we have never bothered to know.

prompt_title: Is It Wrong to Focus on Animal Welfare When Humans Are Suffering?
persona: a retired secondary school teacher who values tradition and discipline
text:
I am not especially surprised that people may feel more immediate pity for a beaten dog than for a beaten adult. A dog seems innocent in a simple, visible way. It cannot explain itself, defend itself, or make sense of cruelty. Many people look at an animal and see trust betrayed. With human beings, unfortunately, we often complicate the matter. We wonder who the person was, what led to the situation, whether there is more to the story. That does not make the suffering less real, but it may make our response less instinctive.

I also think modern life has made many people lonely, and pets have become almost like family members. A dog is loyal, does not argue, and gives affection without conditions. A foreign tourist, in the example, remains an abstraction to some people, while the pet is known and loved. This is understandable, but it is also troubling. A civilized society must teach people to extend sympathy beyond the familiar. That is one of the purposes of education, religion, family life, and good manners: to discipline our feelings so that they do not stop at our own front door.

I do not believe it is wrong to care about animal welfare while humans are suffering. Cruelty to animals is a serious moral failing, and a child who is taught to treat animals kindly learns self-control and compassion. In my years in school, I often found that pupils who tormented weaker creatures needed firm correction, not excuses. How we treat the helpless matters.

However, I do object when concern for animals becomes a way to avoid our duties to human beings. Human life has a special dignity, and we should not forget the elderly neighbor, the neglected child, the poor family, or the stranger in distress. A balanced person can care for both. The proper answer is not to harden our hearts toward animals, but to enlarge them toward people. Compassion, like discipline, should not be selective or sentimental; it should be steady, ordered, and guided by moral responsibility.

prompt_title: Are We Being Bad Citizens If We Don't Keep Up With the News?
persona: a retired secondary school teacher who values tradition and discipline
text:
I do not believe a person must follow every headline to be a good citizen. In fact, I think the modern habit of staring at the news all day can make people anxious, impatient, and poorly informed in a different way. But I do believe that citizens have a duty to know the basic facts of what is happening in their community, their country, and the wider world. Democracy cannot run on ignorance.

When I was teaching, I used to tell my pupils that rights and duties come together. You cannot demand good government, safe streets, decent schools, and honest leadership while refusing to pay attention to the choices being made in your name. Voting, for example, should not be treated like guessing on a test you have not studied for. A citizen ought to know who is standing for office, what they believe, and what the major issues are. That does not require hours of television or endless scrolling. It requires the discipline to read a reliable newspaper, listen to a serious broadcast, or look up information before forming an opinion.

I also think keeping up with the news reminds us that we are not the center of the universe. A flood in another region, a war overseas, a strike at a local hospital, a change in education policy—these things affect real people. Knowing about them can lead to charity, volunteering, letters to representatives, or simply more thoughtful conversation. Not every act changes the world, but a well-informed public creates pressure over time. Leaders behave differently when they know citizens are watching.

At the same time, I have no patience for people who mistake outrage for citizenship. Shouting online, repeating rumors, or treating politics like a sport does little good. Current events should be approached with the same seriousness I expected in my classroom: check your sources, listen before speaking, and be willing to admit when you are wrong.

So yes, we have a responsibility to keep reasonably informed. Not obsessively, not noisily, but steadily. A good citizen need not know everything, but choosing to know nothing is a neglect of duty.

prompt_title: Is Listening to a Book Just as Good as Reading It?
persona: a retired secondary school teacher who values tradition and discipline
text:
I have listened to audiobooks, though I came to them rather late in life. For many years, I regarded “reading” as something done in a chair, with a lamp nearby and a book open in one’s hands. That still seems to me the best and most serious way to meet a text. Yet I have learned that listening to a book can be valuable, and in some circumstances it may be the only practical way for a person to enjoy literature.

Audiobooks are especially useful for busy people, for those with poor eyesight, or for anyone who spends much time travelling. A good narrator can bring out the music of a sentence and the feeling of a scene. I remember teaching Shakespeare and reminding pupils that plays were meant to be heard as well as read. A strong voice can clarify meaning, pace, and emotion. For reluctant readers, listening may also open a door that printed pages have kept closed.

Still, I do not think listening is exactly the same as reading. Reading demands a particular discipline. The eye must follow the line, the mind must hold its place, and the reader must pause, return, and think. When I read a difficult paragraph, I can stop and examine it. I can notice punctuation, spelling, structure, and style. These things matter. They train attention. In a time when many young people are already distracted by constant noise and screens, the quiet patience required by reading is not a small virtue.

Listening can sometimes become too passive. One may wash dishes or walk the dog while a chapter passes by, and afterward remember only half of it. Of course, poor silent reading can be just as careless. The fault is not in the method alone, but in the habits of the person using it.

If I must choose, I prefer reading. I like the weight of a book, the margin of silence around it, and the deliberate effort it asks of me. But I would not scold anyone for listening. Better an audiobook than no book at all. Still, for study, reflection, and the training of the mind, I remain loyal to the printed page.

prompt_title: Should College Athletes Be Paid?
persona: a retired secondary school teacher who values tradition and discipline
text:
College athletes should be treated fairly, but I am not persuaded that turning them into paid employees is the best answer. A scholarship, room and board, medical care, coaching, travel, tutoring and the chance to earn a degree are not small benefits. In my years as a teacher, I saw many young people and families struggle to pay for college at all. For an athlete to receive an education in exchange for representing a school is a serious opportunity, and it ought not be dismissed as if it were nothing.

Cody J. McDavis makes a sensible point when he warns that paying athletes could damage the larger world of college sports. Once money becomes the main measure, the strongest programs will simply outbid everyone else. A few football and basketball players at famous universities may benefit, but what happens to the swimmer, the wrestler, the runner, or the student playing for a small college? Most athletic departments are not wealthy. If schools are forced into a bidding war, they may cut less profitable teams, raise student fees, or place even more pressure on athletes to perform like professionals.

There is also a matter of purpose. College athletics should teach discipline, loyalty, teamwork and perseverance. Those lessons are harder to preserve when students are encouraged to think of themselves primarily as paid entertainers. I do not mean that universities should exploit them. If a player is injured, the school should stand by that student. Scholarships should be guaranteed for a reasonable period, and athletes should be allowed to benefit from their own name and reputation within clear rules. But direct salaries from colleges would change the character of the enterprise.

Tradition is not always perfect, but it often contains wisdom. College sports have long been a bridge between education and competition. We should improve that bridge, not replace it with a marketplace where the richest bidder wins. A college athlete deserves respect, protection and a real education. That is a better goal than a paycheck.

prompt_title: Is It Selfish to Pursue Risky Sports Like Extreme Mountain Climbing?
persona: a retired secondary school teacher who values tradition and discipline
text:
I do not think it is automatically selfish to pursue risky sports such as extreme mountain climbing, but I do think there is a point at which courage becomes vanity and adventure becomes irresponsibility. In my years teaching young people, I often told them that discipline is not the enemy of freedom; it is what makes freedom possible. The same is true in sport.

All sport contains risk. A boy can break his collarbone playing rugby, a girl can suffer a concussion on the hockey field, and even a casual runner may damage a knee. We do not therefore ban sport. Properly taught, sport builds character. It teaches patience, obedience to rules, respect for opponents, and the habit of getting up again after failure. These are old-fashioned virtues perhaps, but they remain necessary.

The question is whether the risk serves a worthy purpose and whether it is accepted responsibly. A trained climber who prepares carefully, respects weather, uses sound equipment, and turns back when conditions demand it is very different from a thrill-seeker chasing a photograph at the summit. The mountain does not care about one’s ambition, and no amount of enthusiasm excuses foolishness. If a person has a spouse, children, pupils, or others who depend on him, he must weigh their claims seriously. To ignore them in pursuit of personal glory is selfish.

I hesitate to say that any activity is too dangerous to be called a sport. Human beings have always tested themselves against nature, and there is something noble in that when done with humility. But some forms of extreme sport seem to have drifted away from sport and toward spectacle. When the main attraction is not skill, endurance, or fair contest, but the real possibility of death, we should be honest about what we are celebrating.

The line, then, is drawn by preparation, purpose, and duty. Risk accepted with discipline may be admirable. Risk pursued for applause, profit, or ego is not bravery. It is recklessness, and no tradition worth preserving requires us to applaud that.

prompt_title: What Are the Most Important Things Students Should Learn in School?
persona: a retired secondary school teacher who values tradition and discipline
text:
In my years as a secondary school teacher, I came to believe that the most important things students should learn in school are not limited to facts in textbooks, though those facts matter greatly. Students should learn to read carefully, write clearly, calculate accurately, and understand the history and culture that shaped their country and the wider world. These are the foundations of an educated mind. A young person who cannot read with attention or express a thought in proper language is at a serious disadvantage, no matter how confident he or she may feel.

Just as important, however, are discipline, punctuality, respect, and perseverance. School is often the first place where children learn that the world does not arrange itself around their convenience. There are deadlines to meet, rules to follow, and standards to uphold. Some people speak of these things as old-fashioned, but I have never seen a successful life built on laziness, excuses, or disorder. A well-kept notebook, a completed assignment, and a respectful manner may seem small, but they form habits that last.

The most important thing I learned in school was the value of self-discipline. I was not the cleverest pupil in every room, but I learned that steady effort could carry a person a long way. A demanding teacher once made us rewrite an essay until every sentence was clear and every error corrected. At the time, I thought it excessive. Later, I understood that he was teaching us pride in our work.

That lesson affected my whole life. It helped me through examinations, military service, teacher training, and decades in the classroom. It taught me not to quit when a task was difficult. In the future, students will face new technologies and changing careers, but the old virtues will still serve them best. Knowledge opens doors, but discipline is what enables a person to walk through them and make something worthy of the opportunity.
